Newly hatched chicks of the Slaty-capped flycatcher emerge from the egg weighing approximately 1.94 grams [Ww0 = approximately 1.94 grams], a modest initial mass that reflects the altricial developmental mode characteristic of this suboscine passerine. The incubation period terminates with hatching at roughly 14 days [ab = roughly 14 days], a duration that was recorded under controlled incubation conditions maintained at a steady 32 °C [T = 32 °C]. This relatively brief embryonic phase is typical of small-bodied tyrant flycatchers and contrasts with the longer incubation periods observed in larger members of the Tyrannidae. During their first days of life, the altricial nestlings are entirely dependent on parental provisioning, and their rapid mass gain is fueled by a diet consisting primarily of small arthropods delivered by both adults. The initial hatchling mass of less than 2 grams represents less than twenty percent of the eventual adult body mass, highlighting the dramatic growth trajectory that must be completed before the chick can achieve independence. Brooding activity by the female is intensive during the first week post-hatching, and the male assumes a substantial role in food delivery during this energetically demanding period. The thermal environment of the nest, buffered by parental incubation behavior, likely moderates the energetic costs of thermoregulation for the developing chicks during these early stages.

As the nestlings progress through the developmental period, they undergo a sustained phase of rapid mass increase before attaining the body dimensions characteristic of a fledgling ready to depart the nest. Adult females reach an asymptotic body mass of approximately 10.5 grams [Wwi = approximately 10.5 grams], while males attain a slightly larger adult size of around 11.5 grams [Wwi = around 11.5 grams] - a modest but consistent sexual size dimorphism that is frequently observed among Neotropical tyrant flycatchers. This dimorphism may be linked to sex-specific differences in the energetic demands of territory defense or courtship displays. The mass gain from the hatchling stage to the adult plateau represents an approximately fivefold increase in female body mass and a nearly sixfold increase in males. Available data indicate that growth rates are highest during the first two weeks post-hatching, with a gradual deceleration as young birds approach adult dimensions. The asymptotic mass is typically reached several weeks after fledging, once the young birds have become proficient at independent foraging and no longer rely on parental food deliveries.

This developmental milestone, marking the age at which the chick first achieves sustained flight and departs the nest cavity, was documented during observations conducted under the thermal conditions typical of active metabolic periods in this species, specifically at an ambient temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. The relatively short nestling period is consistent with the life history strategy of many small-bodied open-cup nesting passerines, where rapid development reduces the window of vulnerability to nest predation. At the time of nest departure, the fledgling possesses fully emerged pin feathers but is not yet capable of sustained flight over long distances, remaining dependent on adults for food for an additional period following independence. The transition from nestling to fledgling is a critical juncture, with mortality rates typically peaking during the first days after leaving the nest. Parental care continues for several weeks post-fledging as the young birds refine their foraging skills and learn to recognize predators.

The onset of sexual maturity in this species is attained relatively early in life, with puberty occurring at approximately 42 days after hatching [tp = approximately 42 days after hatching], a rapid pace of reproductive development that was documented under the same thermal regime of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C] that characterizes the active metabolic period. This accelerated maturation allows young birds to quickly join the breeding population, a trait that may be favored in seasonal environments where the window for successful reproduction is limited. In contrast, the first successful breeding event, representing the age at which a young adult produces its first brood of offspring, is substantially delayed until roughly 365 days after hatching [tR = roughly 365 days after hatching], also recorded at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This decoupling between physiological puberty and actual first reproduction suggests that ecological constraints, such as the need to secure a high-quality territory or develop foraging proficiency, impose a significant delay on reproductive output. First-year birds may attempt breeding later in the season if territories become available, but most successful nesting is undertaken by older, more experienced individuals. The timing of first reproduction has important consequences for population demography, influencing generation time and the rate of population turnover.

The maximum recorded lifespan for the Slaty-capped flycatcher extends to approximately 4015 days [am = approximately 4015 days], a remarkably long duration for a bird of its small body size, which was documented in a longitudinal field study conducted at the species' typical active metabolic temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This longevity is comparable to that of other small Neotropical passerines and likely reflects a relatively low extrinsic mortality rate in stable forest habitats. Associated with this extended lifespan, the species exhibits a conservative reproductive strategy, with females typically laying two eggs per clutch [N_R_i = two eggs per clutch] and producing a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year]. Under the thermal conditions prevalent during the breeding period (40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]), this single-clutch annual strategy contrasts with the double-brooding typical of many temperate tyrannids and likely reflects constraints of the tropical season. The basal metabolic rate of this species, measured through respirometry on resting, post-absorptive individuals under thermoneutral conditions, amounts to 45.45 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 45.45 milliliters of oxygen per hour] at the same ambient temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This metabolic rate is consistent with values reported for other small tyrannids and reflects the energetic demands of maintaining a relatively long lifespan and a slow reproductive pace.
